what_it_does: A new class of chips tries to escape the energy cost of shipping data back and forth between the processor and memory by doing arithmetic directly inside the memory chip itself — 'compute-in-SRAM' (SRAM is the fast on-chip memory that normally just stores numbers). The GSI APU is a real commercial product of this type, packing 2 million tiny 1-bit processors into its memory arrays. This paper is the first to benchmark that chip on practical, large-scale workloads, uncover why naive programs run far below peak speed, and fix the three root causes — achieving GPU-matching retrieval speed at roughly 1% of a GPU's energy.
method_in_detail:
The idea. The GSI APU has extraordinary on-chip memory bandwidth — 26 terabytes per second, roughly 26x a high-end GPU — because the processors and the memory cells share the same silicon. But unlocking that bandwidth requires knowing the chip's quirky internal rules. Its memory is organized into long 'vector registers' (VRs), each holding 32,768 elements. Moving data between two VRs (inter-VR) is cheap and fully parallel; rearranging data inside a single VR (intra-VR) is roughly 10x more expensive.

How it works — three optimizations. First, communication-aware reduction mapping: when computing a dot product (multiplying rows by columns and summing), the naive way assigns the sum over the 'inner' dimension to an intra-VR reduction, which is slow. The paper instead reorders the loops so the reduction happens as a series of element-wise inter-VR additions — one cheap step per column of the matrix rather than one expensive intra-register sum. Second, DMA coalescing: the chip's bulk data-transfer engine (DMA — direct memory access, which moves blocks of data without CPU involvement) was being called repeatedly for the same data chunk at each loop iteration. The fix pre-loads a block once into a reuse register and uses a 'subgroup copy' operation to fill the VR from it, cutting redundant off-chip traffic. Third, broadcast-friendly data layout: the chip looks up scalars from an L3 cache (a slower but larger on-chip store) by fetching a contiguous range. With a row-major data layout, that range can be as large as K*N entries; rearranging data so each lookup window covers only N entries shrinks latency proportionally.

The key design choice. All three optimizations are guided by an analytical model the authors built in Python that predicts latency for any program by summing per-operation costs measured on the real hardware. It predicted Phoenix benchmark latencies to within 6% error on average.

The result. Applied to retrieval-augmented generation — where a language model searches a large library of documents before answering a question — the optimized compute-in-SRAM system searches 200GB of text 6.6x faster than an optimized CPU, matches the end-to-end speed of an NVIDIA A6000 GPU, and consumes 54x to 118x less energy than the GPU across corpus sizes of 10–200 GB.
